entry: American television writer, producer and former attorney. He created or produced series including *Doogie Howser, M.D.*, *Picket Fences*, *Chicago Hope*, *The Practice*, *Boston Legal*, *Ally McBeal*, *Boston Public*, *Goliath* and *Big Little Lies*. His shows have aired on ABC, [[CBS]], Fox, [[NBC]] and [[HBO]]. Kelley practiced law in Boston, mostly in real estate and minor criminal cases, before joining *L.A. Law* as a writer in 1986. In 1999 *Ally McBeal* and *The Practice* won Primetime Emmy Awards for outstanding comedy and drama series.

American filmmaker. He co-founded the production company Propaganda Films in 1986 and directed music videos for [[Madonna]], including "Express Yourself" and "Vogue", both of which won an MTV Video Music Award for Best Direction. His features include *Alien 3* (1992), *Seven* (1995) and *The Social Network* (2010). He received [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations for Best Director for *The Curious Case of Benjamin Button*, *The Social Network* and *Mank*. His films have collectively grossed over $2.1 billion worldwide.

American novelist, essayist and professor. He is best known for *Infinite Jest* (1996), a long novel with numerous endnotes, partly set in a [[Tennis|tennis]] academy. His debut novel, *The Broom of the System* (1987), was followed by story collections such as *Brief Interviews with Hideous Men* (1999) and essays including *Consider the Lobster* (2005). *Everything and More* (2003) examines the history of infinity in [[Set theory|set theory]]. His unfinished novel *The Pale King* (2011) was a finalist for the 2012 [[Pulitzer Prize]] for Fiction.

Canadian and American record producer, composer and songwriter. He has won 16 [[Grammy Awards]] from 45 nominations. Since the 1970s he has composed or produced songs including "I Will Always Love You", "I Have Nothing" and "Hard to Say I'm Sorry", with multiple songs reaching the top spot on the *Billboard* Hot 100. He was nominated three times for the Academy Award for Best Original Song. Foster was senior vice president of Warner Music Group from 1997 and chaired Verve Records from 2012 to 2016. His musical *Boop! The Musical* premiered in Chicago in 2023.

American record executive, film producer and media proprietor. He co-founded Asylum Records with Elliot Roberts in 1971 and founded Geffen Records in 1980. He founded the Geffen Film Company in 1982, and in 1994 he co-founded DreamWorks SKG with [[Steven Spielberg]] and Jeffrey Katzenberg. According to [[Forbes]], Geffen is the wealthiest person in the global entertainment industry, with an estimated net worth of US$9 billion as of 2024.

American actor, singer and television personality. He first gained recognition on the soap opera *The Young and the Restless* (1975–1982), then starred as Michael Knight in *Knight Rider* (1982–1986) and as lifeguard Mitch Buchannon in *Baywatch* (1989–2000), which he also executive produced. His single "Looking for Freedom" reached number one in Germany and [[Switzerland]], and his fifteen studio albums found success mostly in German-speaking Europe. He was a judge on *America's Got Talent* (2006–2009) and *Britain's Got Talent* (2011).

German mathematician and philosopher of mathematics. Hilbert worked on invariant theory, the calculus of variations, commutative algebra, algebraic number theory, the foundations of geometry, spectral theory and mathematical physics, and he co-founded proof theory and [[Mathematical logic|mathematical logic]]. He defended the set theory of [[Georg Cantor]]. His *Grundlagen der Geometrie* (1899) axiomatized [[Euclidean geometry]]. In 1900 he presented 23 problems that set a course for mathematical research in the 20th century. From 1895 he was professor of mathematics at the [[University of Göttingen]], where his students included [[Hermann Weyl]] and Ernst Zermelo and where [[John von Neumann]] served as his assistant.

Scottish philosopher, historian, economist and essayist. Hume's [[Empiricism|empiricism]] and philosophical skepticism were central to his work. In *A Treatise of Human Nature* (1739–40) he argued that all ideas derive from impressions and that causal inference rests on custom and mental habit, since people perceive only the "constant conjunction" of events. Historians usually credit him with first clearly stating the is–ought problem, and he held that ethics rests on sentiment rather than abstract principle. His *History of England* became a bestseller, while his philosophy of religion, including his rejection of miracles, was controversial and his supposed atheism cost him university chairs. [[Immanuel Kant]] said Hume had awakened him from his "dogmatic slumbers".

American preacher and leader of the Branch Davidians, a religious sect. Koresh claimed to be the sect's final prophet. In 1987 he and his followers took over the group's Mount Carmel Center near Waco, [[Texas]]. He faced allegations of [[Polygamy|polygamy]] and child sexual abuse from former associates. A February 1993 raid by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms led to a 51-day standoff, the [[Waco siege]], which ended in a fire. Koresh died of a gunshot wound in unclear circumstances.

English filmmaker and editor, widely considered one of the most important figures of British cinema. Lean began as a film editor in the 1930s before his directorial debut with *In Which We Serve* (1942), the first of four collaborations with Noël Coward. He then directed intimate films such as *Brief Encounter* (1945) and adaptations of [[Charles Dickens]], *Great Expectations* (1946) and *Oliver Twist* (1948). His large-scale epics include *The Bridge on the River Kwai* (1957), *Lawrence of Arabia* (1962), *Doctor Zhivago* (1965) and *A Passage to India* (1984), which was his last film. Lean won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Director for *The Bridge on the River Kwai* and *Lawrence of Arabia*. After the critical failure of *Ryan's Daughter* (1970), he took a fourteen-year break from filmmaking.

American comedian, television host and producer. He hosted late-night talk shows for 33 years, first *Late Night with David Letterman* on [[NBC]] from 1982 and then *Late Show with David Letterman* on [[CBS]] until 2015. He hosted 6,080 episodes in total, surpassing his mentor [[Johnny Carson]] as the longest-serving late-night talk show host in American television history. His company, Worldwide Pants, produced *Everybody Loves Raymond*. Late-night hosts including [[Conan O'Brien]] and Stephen Colbert have cited his influence.

Scottish doctor, missionary and explorer of Africa. Working with the London Missionary Society, Livingstone explored the African interior and mapped much of central Africa. He sought the sources of the [[Nile]] in the belief that fame from the discovery would give him influence to end the East African slave trade. His travels included the identification of [[Victoria Falls]]. He documented Arab and Portuguese slaving networks and advocated their suppression. He died of dysentery and malaria in what is now [[Zambia]], and his body was returned to Britain for burial in [[Westminster Abbey]]. His death made him a national hero and helped inspire missionary initiatives in central Africa during the [[Scramble for Africa]].

Welsh Liberal politician, prime minister of the United Kingdom, 1916–22. As chancellor of the exchequer from 1908 to 1915 he introduced the 1909 People's Budget, whose taxes on land and high incomes led to the Parliament Act 1911 curtailing the veto of the [[House of Lords]]. His National Insurance Act 1911 helped establish the modern [[Welfare state|welfare state]]. As minister of munitions from 1915 he expanded shell production, and in December 1916 he replaced H. H. Asquith as prime minister. He centralized authority in a smaller war cabinet and introduced the convoy system against [[U-boat|U-boats]]. He was a leading participant at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference and negotiated independence for the Irish Free State in 1921, though his government was dogged by a scandal over the sale of honors. The Conservatives ended the coalition in 1922, and he resigned.

American filmmaker and artist. His films are characterized by a surrealist sensibility that gave rise to the adjective "Lynchian". His feature debut, the body-horror film *Eraserhead* (1977), was followed by *The Elephant Man* (1980), *Blue Velvet* (1986) and *Mulholland Drive* (2001), each of which earned him an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nomination for Best Director. *Wild at Heart* (1990) won the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival]]. With Mark Frost he co-created the ABC series *Twin Peaks* (1990–1991; 2017), which is often listed among the greatest television series. He also directed *Dune* (1984), which he later disowned after studio interference, and *Inland Empire* (2006), his last feature film. A longtime practitioner of Transcendental Meditation, he founded the David Lynch Foundation.

American playwright, author and filmmaker. He won a [[Pulitzer Prize]] for *Glengarry Glen Ross* (1983). His other plays include *American Buffalo* and *Speed-the-Plow* (1988), and he wrote and directed films including *House of Games* (1987), *The Spanish Prisoner* (1997) and *Heist* (2001). He wrote the screenplays for *The Postman Always Rings Twice* (1981) and *The Verdict* (1982). He created and produced the [[CBS]] series *The Unit* (2006–2009). His 2011 book *The Secret Knowledge: On the Dismantling of American Culture* is a commentary on cultural and political issues.

Renaissance marble statue in Florence, Italy, by [[Michelangelo]]. Michelangelo carved the statue, 5.17 m high, from a very large block of marble between 1501 and 1504. Earlier sculptors had begun work on the block, which was originally intended for a series of prophets on the roofline of the [[Florence Cathedral|cathedral]]. The statue was instead unveiled in the Piazza della Signoria on September 8, 1504. It became a symbol of the civil liberties of the Florentine republic, which faced threats from more powerful rivals and from the Medici family. It was the first colossal marble statue of the High Renaissance and the first since [[Classical antiquity|classical antiquity]]. The statue was moved to the Galleria dell'Accademia in 1873, and a replica stands on its original site.

English actor, memoirist and novelist. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *Separate Tables* (1958), a record for the shortest winning performance in the category, at 23 minutes and 39 seconds. He rejoined the army in the [[World War II|Second World War]] and co-starred in *The First of the Few* (1942). His other films include *Around the World in 80 Days* (1956), *The Pink Panther* (1963), in which he played Sir Charles Lytton, and *Casino Royale* (1967), in which he played James Bond. His memoir *The Moon's a Balloon* (1971) was a bestseller.

British economist and politician. A leading classical economist, Ricardo worked alongside [[Adam Smith]] and others in shaping the field. He introduced the concept of comparative advantage, holding that nations should concentrate resources in the industries where they are most efficient relative to their alternative uses. He argued that international trade is always beneficial, even when one country is more competitive in every area. He opposed the Corn Laws and [[Protectionism|protectionism]]. He revised Adam Smith's labor theory of value and developed theories of rent, wages and profits. Elected to Parliament for Portarlington in 1819, he advocated parliamentary reform and free trade. His *On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation* (1817) set out these ideas.

Scottish actor known for playing the Tenth Doctor in *Doctor Who*. He starred in the role from 2005 to 2010 and returned as the Fourteenth Doctor in 2023. His other television roles include DI Alec Hardy in *Broadchurch* (2013–2017) and Kilgrave in *Jessica Jones* (2015–2019). On stage he has worked extensively with the Royal Shakespeare Company, including *Hamlet* (2008–2009) and *Richard II* (2013, 2016). His accolades include two BAFTA Scotland Awards and two Emmy Awards.

American politician and frontiersman. He represented Tennessee in the [[United States House of Representatives]] from 1827 to 1831 and from 1833 to 1835, opposing President [[Andrew Jackson]]'s Indian Removal Act. After losing his seat in 1835 he went to [[Texas]] and fought in the Texas Revolution. He died at the [[Battle of the Alamo]], and accounts differ on whether he was killed in combat or executed after capture. Stories of his larger-than-life exploits, popularized by stage plays and almanacs, made him one of the best-known American folk heroes.

Indian-born Pakistani gangster and crime boss. He founded the criminal syndicate D-Company in [[Mumbai]] in the 1970s and fled to [[Dubai]] in 1986. He is wanted on charges including murder, extortion and terrorism. He is widely believed to have masterminded the 1993 Bombay bombings, and in 2003 the [[United Nations Security Council]] and the United States designated him a global terrorist. The United States has a bounty of US$25 million on him. He is reported to live in [[Karachi]], Pakistan, a claim the Pakistani government denies.

Mexican holiday honoring deceased family and friends. Traditionally held on November 1 and 2, the multi-day holiday involves visiting graves and building home [[Altar|altars]] called *ofrendas*, stocked with the favorite foods and drinks of the dead. Marigolds and sugar skulls (*calaveras*) are common, and celebrants share humorous anecdotes about the departed. Scholars disagree on its origins: some argue for Indigenous Mexican or Aztec influences, while others see a local form of the Spanish Allhallowtide season. In 2008 [[UNESCO]] added the festival to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

Practice of advancing clocks by one hour in spring and setting them back in autumn. Daylight saving time (DST) makes better use of summer daylight by moving darkness to a later clock time, hence the mnemonic "spring forward, fall back". The first local implementation was in Port Arthur and Fort William, Ontario, [[Canada]], in 1908, and the first nationwide ones were by the German and Austro-Hungarian Empires, starting April 30, 1916. As of 2023 around 34 percent of the world's countries used DST, mainly in Europe and North America. The [[United States|U.S.]] and Russia both tried permanent DST only briefly, and the U.S. then returned to seasonal DST while Russia switched to permanent standard time. In a satirical 1784 letter, [[Benjamin Franklin]] suggested that Parisians wake earlier in summer to save candles, but he did not propose changing clocks.

American daytime television [[Soap opera|soap opera]]. Created by husband-and-wife team Ted Corday and Betty Corday, the show premiered on [[NBC]] on November 8, 1965, and is set in the fictional town of Salem, [[Illinois]]. It centers on the Brady and Horton families. Daily episodes were expanded from 30 to 60 minutes in 1975. The soap moved exclusively to the Peacock streaming service in September 2022, after 57 years on NBC. It celebrated its 15,000th episode on December 2, 2024, and has been renewed through 2028.

City and county seat of Montgomery County, Ohio, United States. Founded in 1796 on the Great Miami River and named for Jonathan Dayton, a signer of the U.S. Constitution, it grew in the 19th century as a canal town. It was home to many inventors, notably the [[Wright brothers]], who developed the first successful motor-operated airplane. Later the city hosted the Dayton Project, a branch of the [[Manhattan Project]] that developed polonium triggers for early atomic bombs. The city had 137,644 residents at the 2020 census and is a logistics hub near Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.
